topics.title: Sustainable Agriculture
topics.definition: Agriculture that meets present needs without endangering the resource base of future generations.

sections.heading: Core features
content: Prevents land degradation and soil erosion.
Replenishes nutrients in the soil.
Controls weeds, pests and diseases through biological and cultural methods.
Minimizes dependence on synthetic fertilizers, pesticides and antibiotics.
Uses manures, crop rotation and minimal tillage.

sections.heading: Also known as
content: Alternative farming
Regenerative agriculture
Natural or organic farming
Eco-farming
Permeaculture

topics.title: Sustainability in Agriculture
topics.definition: The capacity of agriculture to remain productive while maintaining its resource base.

sections.heading: Five characteristics
content: Ecologically sound: soil, crop, animal and human health are maintained.
Economically viable: farmers can produce enough for self-sufficiency.
Socially just: basic needs and productive resources are fairly accessed.
Humane: plant, animal and human life are respected.
Adaptable: rural communities can adjust to changing farming conditions.

sections.heading: WCED 1987 concept
content: Today's economic development should not be at the expense of tomorrow's development prospects.

topics.title: Sustainable Agriculture vs Modern Agriculture
topics.definition: The source contrasts resource-conserving sustainable agriculture with chemical-input-based modern agriculture.

sections.heading: Plant nutrients
content: Sustainable: farmyard manure, compost, green manure, biofertilizers and crop rotations.
Modern: chemical fertilizers.

sections.heading: Pest control
content: Sustainable: cultural, crop rotation and biological methods.
Modern: toxic chemicals.

sections.heading: Inputs and ecology
content: Sustainable: diverse, renewable and biodegradable inputs; stable ecology.
Modern: high productivity with lower diversity and fragile ecology.

sections.heading: Resource extraction
content: Sustainable: extraction should not exceed regeneration.
Modern: extraction may exceed regeneration.

sections.heading: Food material
content: Sustainable: food materials are presented as safe.
Modern: food materials may contain toxic residues.

topics.title: Problems of Modern Agriculture
topics.definition: Environmental problems associated in the source with modern agricultural development and faulty practices.

sections.heading: Major problems
content: Ozone layer damage from atmospheric pollutants such as CFC, nitrogen oxide and methane.
Increasing CO2 contributes to global warming, sea-level rise and rainfall-pattern changes.
Water and wind erosion cause loss of productive soil.
Deforestation increases erosion, floods, reservoir siltation and runoff.
Improper irrigation may cause soil salinization and alkalization.
Excessive groundwater extraction depletes groundwater.
Pesticide and fertilizer residues pollute surface and groundwater.
Biological diversity is reduced.

topics.title: Major Components of Sustainable Agriculture
topics.definition: Resource and crop-management practices used to sustain productivity while reducing environmental damage.

sections.heading: Components
content: Soil and water conservation prevents degradation and can extend the crop-growing season.
Efficient irrigation-water use reduces salinity, alkalinity and high water-table problems.
Crop rotations reduce insect-pests, diseases and weeds.
Crop rotations improve soil productivity and reduce erosion.
Integrated nutrient management combines organic, inorganic and biological nutrient sources.
Integrated pest management reduces dependence on agrochemicals.
Good weed management uses preventive measures, tillage, timely intercultivation and crop rotation.

topics.title: Goals of Sustainable Agriculture
topics.definition: Long-term production goals based on resource conservation and efficient use.

sections.heading: Goals
content: Use nutrient cycling and nitrogen fixation.
Reduce external and non-renewable inputs.
Improve equitable access to productive resources and opportunities.
Use the biological and genetic potential of plants and animals.
Maintain current production levels over the long term.
Integrate farm management with conservation of soil, water, energy and biological resources.

topics.title: Factors Affecting Ecological Balance
topics.definition: Major land, water and input-management factors that disturb ecological balance.

sections.heading: Major factors
content: Deforestation and overgrazing reduce vegetation, alter climate and biodiversity, and cause resource loss.
Loss of vegetative cover accelerates soil erosion.
Poor-quality irrigation water and poor drainage cause salinity and sodicity.
Over-extraction of groundwater lowers the water table.
Over-irrigation can accumulate harmful salts.
Excess fertilizer use reduces soil biological activity and contributes to nitrate pollution.
Pesticides can cause resistance and environmental contamination.

topics.title: Soil Management for Sustainable Agriculture
topics.definition: Practices for preventing soil degradation and restoring productive capacity.

sections.heading: Soil degradation
content: Water and wind erosion are major causes.
Chemical degradation includes salinization and loss of nutrients and organic matter.
Short- and long-term measures are required.

sections.heading: Conservation practices
content: Contour farming.
Agronomic and cultural measures.
Contour bunding and graded bunding.
Contour ditches and bench terracing.
Runoff cycling.
Alternative land use such as pasture and fuel-fodder-timber systems on non-agricultural land.

sections.heading: Watershed approach
content: Stores drainage water for recycling.
Stored water can support crops during drought.
Can improve rainfed-crop productivity.

topics.title: Integrated Nutrient Management (INM)
topics.definition: A nutrient-management approach that minimizes chemical use and improves nutrient-use efficiency.

sections.heading: Main components
content: Recycle crop residues and animal wastes.
Use composting and vermicomposting for materials unsuitable for direct application.
Use biological nitrogen fixation through BGA, Azolla, Rhizobium, Azotobacter and Azospirillum.
Use phosphate-solubilizing microorganisms.
Use green manuring to improve fertility and supply nutrients.
Include legumes in rotations and intercropping.
Biogas plants and suitable sewage/sludge use can contribute to nutrient recycling.

sections.heading: Green manure examples
content: Sesbania aculeata (Dhaincha).
Crotalaria juncea (Sannhemp).
Sesbania rostrata.

sections.heading: Sesbania rostrata
content: Source states fixation of about 100–250 kg N/ha in 45–55 days.

topics.title: Management of Water Resources
topics.definition: Efficient use, conservation and recharge of irrigation and other water resources.

sections.heading: Recommendations
content: Use proper land shaping and leveling.
Use efficient irrigation-system design.
Use pipe channels to reduce seepage losses.
Use furrow, alternate-furrow or skip-furrow irrigation for row crops.
Use sprinkler and drip systems in water-scarce areas.
Use surface and groundwater conjunctively.
Provide drainage in canal command areas.
Use suitable cropping systems instead of continuous lowland rice.
Use recommended crop-production technology.
Develop integrated watersheds.
Recharge groundwater using basins, recharge wells, check dams and percolation ponds.

topics.title: Management of Rainwater
topics.definition: Planned use and conservation of rainfall for sustainable crop production.

sections.heading: Source facts
content: Rainfall varies widely across space and time.
The source states about 70% of India's cultivated area depends entirely on rainfall.

sections.heading: Options
content: Use agro-climatic analysis to assess rainfall probability.
Select cropping systems based on agro-climatic conditions.
Prepare contingency crop plans for abnormal weather.
Use improved soil and water management.
Conserve soil moisture in situ.
Harvest and recycle runoff.
Use improved management packages for cropping systems.

topics.title: Integrated Pest Management (IPM)
topics.definition: A combination of agronomic, biological, chemical, physical and other methods that keeps harmful organisms at economically insignificant levels with minimum interference to beneficial organisms.

sections.heading: Core principle
content: Bio-agents are an integral part of IPM.
Priority is given to methods that reduce unnecessary pesticide dependence.

sections.heading: Examples
content: Predator: Coccinella spp.
Parasitoid: Trichogramma species.

sections.heading: Agronomic components
content: Land preparation can create unfavorable conditions for pests, diseases and weeds.
Select resistant or tolerant cultivars.
Adjust sowing time to escape peak pest pressure.
Avoid excessively dense plant populations.
Use mechanical or manual intercultivation.
Apply balanced NPK; excessive nitrogen may increase crop succulence.
Manage irrigation and drainage to avoid pest and disease build-up.
Use intercropping.
Use crop rotation.

topics.title: Land Degradation
topics.definition: Loss of soil productivity or a process that lowers current or potential soil capacity to produce.

sections.heading: Source figures
content: About 32.7% of the total geographical area is stated as degraded.
Total geographical area: 328.73 million ha.
About 65% of land degradation occurs through water and wind erosion.
Net sown area: 141.89 million ha.

sections.heading: Types and area
content: Water erosion: 57.16 mha.
Wind erosion: 10.46 mha.
Ravines: 2.68 mha.
Salt affected: 6.32 mha.
Water logging: 3.20 mha.
Mines and quarry wastes: 0.25 mha.
Shifting cultivation: 2.35 mha.
Degraded forest: 24.9 mha.
Special problems: 0.09 mha.
Total listed degraded area: 107.43 mha.

topics.title: Types of Soil Degradation
topics.definition: Soil degradation is classified in the source as physical, chemical and biological degradation.

sections.heading: Physical degradation
content: Soil erosion.
Soil slips.
Soil slides.
Mud flow.
Water logging.

sections.heading: Chemical degradation
content: Soil salinity.
Soil sodicity.
Soil acidity.

sections.heading: Biological degradation
content: Loss of soil organic matter.
Associated with high temperature and low water content.

topics.title: Major Factors Affecting Land Degradation
topics.definition: Human, environmental and management pressures that reduce land quality.

sections.heading: Factors
content: Extensive and frequent cropping.
Excessive fertilizer use.
Shifting cultivation without adequate recovery.
Poor irrigation practices.
Over-extraction of groundwater.
Conversion of forest and agricultural land to other uses.
Urban encroachment.
Deforestation and illegal felling.
Overgrazing and excessive fuel-wood collection.
Industrial and mining activities without adequate preventive measures.
Human and livestock pressure.
Frequent drought or monsoon failure.

topics.title: Soil Erosion
topics.definition: Detachment of soil particles from the parent soil body.

sections.heading: Types
content: Wind erosion.
Water erosion.
Wave erosion.

sections.heading: Wave erosion
content: Caused by combined action of wind and water.
Occurs mainly along canal and river banks.
Can be controlled by lining canals.

sections.heading: Basic relationship
content: Erosion = f(erosivity) × (erodibility).
Erosivity is the potential ability of rain to cause erosion.
Erodibility is soil vulnerability to erosion based on inherent properties.

topics.title: Factors and Losses Due to Soil Erosion
topics.definition: Rainfall, vegetation and soil properties control erosion and its effects.

sections.heading: Factors
content: Rainfall amount, intensity, duration and distribution affect runoff and erosion.
Vegetative cover intercepts rainfall and reduces erosion.
Topography affects runoff and particle transport.
Increasing slope generally increases erosion.

sections.heading: Major losses
content: Loss of rainwater from fields.
Loss of fertile topsoil.
Loss of plant nutrients.
Siltation of reservoirs and reduced storage capacity.

sections.heading: Source figures
content: Soil loss is stated as 16.35 t/ha annually.
Permissible limit is stated as 11 t/ha.

topics.title: Water Erosion and USLE
topics.definition: Water erosion is described through sheet, rill and gully stages; USLE is used to predict soil loss.

sections.heading: Stages
content: Sheet erosion: uniform removal of a thin topsoil layer.
Rill erosion: small channels formed by runoff.
Gully erosion: advanced rill stage with deep and wide channels.

sections.heading: USLE
content: A = R K L S C P.
A = predicted soil loss.
R = rainfall and runoff factor.
K = soil erodibility.
L = slope length.
S = slope gradient.
C = soil cover and management.
P = erosion-control practice.

topics.title: Wind Erosion
topics.definition: Wind-driven movement of soil particles through saltation, suspension and surface creep.

sections.heading: Particle movement
content: Saltation: bouncing of fine particles around 0.1–0.5 mm.
Suspension: movement of very fine particles or dust below 0.1 mm.
Surface creep: movement of particles above 0.5 mm and below 1.0 mm along the surface.

sections.heading: Factors
content: Wind velocity is a major factor.
The source states wind velocity above 5–6 m/s is undesirable.
Soil texture, structure, cohesiveness, bulk density, organic matter, moisture and surface roughness affect erosion.
Vegetative cover reduces erosion.

sections.heading: Wind erosion equation
content: E = I R K F C W D B.
E = soil loss by wind erosion.
I = soil cloudiness factor.
R = surface cover factor.
K = surface roughness factor.
F = soil textural class factor.
C = local wind factor.
W = field width factor.
D = wind direction factor.
B = wind barrier factor.

topics.title: Natural Resource Management
topics.definition: A sustainable-agriculture approach focused on efficient use and conservation of limited natural resources.

sections.heading: Need
content: Green Revolution increased food production, but sustainability is now a major concern.
Limited land and water resources require continuous productivity improvement.
Poor resource management and excessive agrochemicals threaten sustainability.
Impacts include biodiversity loss, land and water degradation, pollution and climatic changes.

sections.heading: Water-resource pressures
content: Limited expansion of irrigation potential.
Non-judicious use of water.
Poor irrigation-project efficiency, stated as only 30–40%.
Conveyance losses.
Diversion of agricultural water to non-agricultural uses.
Increasing groundwater pollution.

topics.title: Strategies for Natural Resource Management
topics.definition: Resource-conservation strategies for maintaining agricultural productivity and ecological balance.

sections.heading: Biological diversity
content: Maintain essential ecological processes.
Preserve genetic diversity.
Ensure sustainable use of species and ecosystems.

sections.heading: Diversification
content: Use crop diversification.
Integrate dairy, fisheries, poultry, horticulture and forestry.
Reduce monoculture effects.
Improve soil health and resource use.
Support nutrient recycling.
Reduce risk and uncertainty.

sections.heading: Improved systems
content: Integrated intensive farming system uses farm-grown biological inputs and nutrient recycling.
Precision farming improves input-use efficiency.
Use soil-test-based fertilizer application.
Use land leveling and micro-irrigation.
Include legumes in crop rotations.

sections.heading: Other measures
content: Use organic farming.
Reclaim degraded land.
Use integrated water management.
Use bio-intensive integrated pest management.

topics.title: High External Input Agriculture (HEIA)
topics.definition: An agricultural system dependent on substantial external inputs such as hybrid seed, fertilizers, pesticides, machinery and irrigation.

sections.heading: Development
content: Developed in response to rising food demand.
Green Revolution emphasized higher harvest per unit area and increased cropping seasons.
High-yielding hybrid varieties required new production practices.

sections.heading: Input dependence
content: Chemical fertilizers were used heavily because hybrid varieties were nutrient sensitive.
Pesticides were needed because new crops were susceptible to pests and diseases.
Weedicides or manual weeding were needed because dwarf hybrids competed poorly with weeds.
Mechanization became an integral component.
New crops required more water and improved irrigation.

sections.heading: Sustainability issue
content: Many external resources were not recycled.
The system depended on regular external inputs for high yields.
Stopping inputs could make the system unproductive.

topics.title: Advantages of HEIA
topics.definition: Benefits attributed in the source to high external input agriculture.

sections.heading: Advantages
content: Rapid increase in agricultural production.
Improved food availability.
Reduction of some nutrition-related problems.
Improved varieties can give yields in a short period.
Mechanization helps address labour shortages.
Higher income and profit margins.
Higher land productivity.
Improved market facilities.

topics.title: Disadvantages of HEIA
topics.definition: Environmental, economic and social problems associated in the source with high external input agriculture.

sections.heading: Major disadvantages
content: Reduced biodiversity can disturb environmental balance.
Machinery may increase soil erosion through constant furrowing.
Dependence on imported machinery, fertilizers, pesticides and hybrid seed.
Pesticides can kill natural enemies as well as target pests.
Agrochemicals can affect soil pH, CEC, structure, texture and soil organisms.
High capital requirements can disadvantage capital-poor farmers.
Traditional varieties and indigenous knowledge may decline.
Farmers may face environmental, social and economic problems.

topics.title: Limitations of Green Revolution Practices
topics.definition: Shortcomings identified by the source in planning and long-term effects of Green Revolution practices.

sections.heading: Economic and ecological issues
content: Surplus production could contribute to lower commodity prices.
Long-term dependence on pesticides and chemical fertilizers was not fully anticipated.
Quick crop response encouraged artificial-manure use without awareness of long-term effects.
The source states that 40–50% of applied nitrogen may be wasted in tropical countries.
Nitrogen losses increase with high rainfall, drought, erosion and low organic matter.
Continuous NPK use may create micronutrient deficiencies.
Nitrous oxide contributes to atmospheric and ozone-related concerns.

sections.heading: Pesticide issues
content: Pesticide poisoning can affect people.
Repeated use can lead to pest resistance.
Pesticides can kill natural enemies.
Pesticides can contaminate water, air, soil and food.
Pesticides can enter food chains and food webs.

topics.title: Low External Input and Sustainable Agriculture (LEISA)
topics.definition: An integrated agricultural system designed to maintain optimum production using fewer external inputs in an eco-friendly manner.

sections.heading: Need
content: Developed in response to high capital needs and environmental impacts of HEIA.
Combines selected traditional principles with newer technology.
The source describes LEISA as integrating bio-dynamic, environmental, natural, organic and regenerative subsystems.

sections.heading: Ecological principles
content: Maintain favorable soil conditions and stimulate soil microorganisms.
Maintain nutrient balance through fixation, deep nutrient use, recycling and needed supplementation.
Control microclimate-related resource losses.
Use biological and mechanical erosion control.
Prioritize natural biological pest control.
Promote biodiversity and plant–plant and plant–animal interactions.

sections.heading: Core practices
content: Maintain a living soil.
Create biodiversity.
Recycle resources.
Use natural pest management.

topics.title: Living Soil and Soil Organisms
topics.definition: LEISA emphasizes maintaining the biological, physical and chemical characteristics needed for productive soil.

sections.heading: Requirements
content: Adequate water, air and nutrients.
Favorable soil structure for water, nutrients and root growth.
Suitable soil temperature.
Absence of poisonous substances.
Active soil microorganisms.

sections.heading: Soil organisms
content: Microflora: bacteria, fungi and algae.
Microfauna: protozoa.
Mesofauna: nematodes.
Macro animals: weevils, centipedes, termites, rats, worms and snakes.

sections.heading: Microorganism functions
content: Decompose organic matter into humus.
Mineralize humus and release nutrients.
Assist nitrogen fixation.
Convert insoluble phosphate to soluble forms.
Help plants absorb nutrients.
Maintain soil sanitation.
Help suppress harmful microorganisms.

topics.title: Resource Cycling and Recycling
topics.definition: Reuse of farm outputs and residues as inputs to maintain nutrient balance and reduce external-input dependence.

sections.heading: Nutrient balance
content: Nutrient removal should not exceed nutrient inflow.
Natural recycling can maintain nutrient balance when not disturbed.
Nitrogen fixation, organic manure, suitable fertilizer combinations and crop rotations support recycling.

sections.heading: Farm examples
content: Paddy straw can be recycled as a nutrient source.
Maize residues can be returned to the soil.
Dairy wastes can become manure.
Crop and livestock enterprises can exchange outputs and inputs.

topics.title: Natural Crop Protection Methods
topics.definition: Preventive, biological, mechanical and natural-product methods used to manage pests in sustainable systems.

sections.heading: Preventive measures
content: Treat seed and planting material before planting.
Use hot-water treatment where suitable.
Use wood ash and sun drying where appropriate.
Maintain hygiene of farm implements.
Remove infested fruits, plants, ratoons and host plants.

sections.heading: Crop resistance
content: Select varieties resistant to pests and diseases.
Use multiple cropping to promote natural predators.

sections.heading: Methods
content: Biological control.
Mechanical control.
Natural pesticides.
Artificial pesticides when included within the listed integrated methods.

sections.heading: Natural pesticide examples
content: Garlic.
Big onion.
Pepper.
Tobacco.
Neem.

topics.title: Major Irrigation Problems
topics.definition: Problems caused by excessive irrigation, poor water quality, high water tables and inadequate drainage.

sections.heading: Major problems
content: Soil salinity.
Soil alkalinity.
High water table.
Poor drainage.

sections.heading: Main causes
content: Saline irrigation water.
Salt deposition from a high water table.
Canal seepage.
Arid climate.
Poor drainage.
Backwater flow in coastal areas.

sections.heading: Controlling factors
content: Quality of irrigation water.
Irrigation frequency.
Soil type and permeability.
Crop salt tolerance.
Climate.

topics.title: Saline and Alkali Soils
topics.definition: Salt-affected soils distinguished in the source using EC, ESP, pH, salt composition and physical condition.

sections.heading: USDA classification
content: Saline: EC >4 mmhos/cm; ESP <15; pH <8.5.
Saline-alkali: EC >4; ESP >15; pH >8.5.
Alkali: EC <4; ESP >15; pH 8.5–10.0.

sections.heading: Saline soil
content: Common in arid and semi-arid areas.
Favored by high water table, high salt concentration, high temperature and low rainfall.
Main soluble salts include chlorides and sulphates.
ESP is below 15%; pH is below 8.5.
EC is above 4 mmho/cm.
Generally flocculated with relatively normal aeration and permeability.
Can be reclaimed mainly through leaching and ponding.

sections.heading: Alkali soil
content: Common in Indo-Gangetic plains and poorly drained low-lying areas.
Carbonates mainly involve sodium.
ESP is above 15%; pH is above 8.5.
EC is below 4 mmho/cm.
Soil is dispersed and compact with poor aeration and permeability.
Amendments such as gypsum or iron pyrite are important.

sections.heading: Formulas
content: ESP = exchangeable sodium / total cation exchange capacity × 100.
SAR = Na+ / √(Ca2+ + Mg2+) .

topics.title: Wasteland: Meaning and Classification
topics.definition: Land that is unproductive or underutilized because of neglect, degradation or constraints, though some wastelands can be reclaimed.

sections.heading: Definitions
content: Wasteland Survey and Reclamation Committee (1961): lands unavailable for cultivation or left as fallows and cultivable wastes.
National Wasteland Development Board: lands currently unutilized due to different constraints.
Wastelands include culturable and unculturable categories.
They are also termed degraded lands.

sections.heading: Classification
content: Culturable wastelands have potential for vegetative cover but face constraints such as erosion, waterlogging and salinization.
Many culturable wastelands can be made productive through treatment and reclamation.
Unculturable wastelands cannot be developed for vegetative cover, such as barren rocky or snow-covered areas.

sections.heading: Source figure
content: About 158 mha of India's 329 mha geographical area is stated as being under different kinds of land degradation.

topics.title: Management of Wastelands
topics.definition: Site-specific reclamation and vegetation measures for degraded and underutilized lands.

sections.heading: Ravine land
content: River erosion and deposition create ravine lands.
Known locally as khadar, diara, char, rao and cho in different regions.
Use soil-conservation measures.
Live hedges help control erosion and sediment deposition.

sections.heading: Coastal sandy areas
content: Afforestation is recommended.
Wide forest belts can moderate cyclone effects.
Casuarina tolerates salinity and moisture stress.

sections.heading: High-altitude and steep slopes
content: Excess runoff during monsoon can cause erosion and floods.
Dry periods may create moisture deficiency.
Indiscriminate grazing is a major erosion cause.
Use hedgerow planting and suitable agroforestry trees and shrubs.

topics.title: Organic Farming
topics.definition: A farming system that largely excludes synthetic inputs and relies on ecological processes, organic resources, crop rotations and biological nutrient and pest management.

sections.heading: Concept
content: Organic farming has been practiced in India since ancient times.
Aims to regenerate natural processes and make the farm ecosystem self-sustainable.
Organic components vary with crop, region and time.
The common goal is continued production through a self-supporting system.

sections.heading: USDA definition in source
content: Avoids or largely excludes synthetic fertilizers, pesticides, hormones and feed additives.
Relies on crop rotations, crop residues, animal manures, off-farm organic waste, mineral-grade rock additives and biological nutrient and plant-protection systems.

sections.heading: Aims
content: Work within a closed system using local resources.
Maintain long-term soil productivity.
Avoid agrochemical pollution.
Minimize fossil-energy use.

topics.title: Principles of Organic Farming
topics.definition: Principles that guide nutrient supply, pest management, biological nitrogen fixation and biomass recycling in organic farming.

sections.heading: Core principles
content: Crops should obtain nutrients through soil biological activity under suitable conditions.
Pests and diseases should be controlled mainly through natural enemies, predators, biological agents and natural products.
Organic sources may be used in digested, semi-digested or undigested forms.
Natural resistance of crops to pests and diseases should be utilized.
Biological nitrogen fixation should be encouraged.
Biomass management should support a self-supporting nutrient system.

sections.heading: IFOAM-style principles presented in source
content: Principle of health.
Principle of ecology.
Principle of fairness.
Principle of care.

topics.title: Components of Organic Farming
topics.definition: Major biological and organic inputs used for nutrient supply and soil management.

sections.heading: Biofertilizers
content: Contain selected microorganisms.
May fix atmospheric nitrogen or make insoluble phosphorus available.
Are described as cost-effective, eco-friendly and renewable nutrient sources.

sections.heading: Major groups
content: Free-living nitrogen fixers.
Symbiotic nitrogen fixers.
Associative symbiotic organisms such as Azospirillum.
Phosphorus-solubilizing bacteria and fungi.
Arbuscular and ectomycorrhiza.

sections.heading: Other biological inputs
content: Azolla.
Plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR).
Mycorrhizal fungi.

topics.title: Important Biofertilizers and Microbial Inputs
topics.definition: Microbial inoculants used for nitrogen fixation, phosphorus mobilization and plant growth support.

sections.heading: Nitrogen-fixing groups
content: Azotobacter: free-living nitrogen fixer.
Rhizobium: symbiotic association with legumes.
Azospirillum: associative symbiotic nitrogen fixer of graminaceous plants.
Azolla: free-floating fern capable of fixing atmospheric nitrogen.

sections.heading: Phosphorus-related inputs
content: Bacillus spp. and Aspergillus niger can solubilize unavailable phosphorus.
Mycorrhiza assists nutrient transfer, especially phosphorus, and may also help zinc and sulphur transfer.

sections.heading: PGPR
content: Colonize roots or rhizosphere soil.
Benefit crops through growth-promoting effects.
Some produce phytohormones and are used as biostimulants.

topics.title: Organic Manures
topics.definition: Organic materials used to supply nutrients and improve soil physical and biological properties.

sections.heading: Sources
content: Cattle shed wastes.
Human habitation wastes.
Poultry litter and sheep/goat droppings.
Slaughterhouse wastes.
Agro-industry by-products.
Crop residues.
Water hyacinth, weeds and tank silt.
Green manure and green-leaf material.

sections.heading: Groups
content: Bulky organic manures.
Concentrated organic manures.

sections.heading: Benefits of bulky manures
content: Supply plant nutrients including micronutrients.
Improve soil structure and water-holding capacity.
Increase nutrient availability.
Influence soil biological activity during decomposition.

topics.title: Farmyard Manure (FYM)
topics.definition: Decomposed mixture of dung and urine of farm animals with associated litter and refuse.

sections.heading: Preparation
content: Trenches are described as about 6 m long, 2 m wide and 1 m deep.
Dung and urine-soaked material is collected daily.
Litter and refuse are mixed with soil to absorb urine.
Collected material is placed in the trench in sections.

sections.heading: Use
content: Partially rotten FYM should be applied about 3–4 weeks before sowing.
Manure left exposed in the field for long periods may lose nutrients.
Immediate incorporation after spreading reduces losses.
Responsive crops listed include potato, tomato, sweet potato, carrot, radish, onion, sugarcane, rice, Napier grass and several orchard crops.

topics.title: Composting Methods
topics.definition: Controlled decomposition of organic wastes into a stable manure-like material.

sections.heading: Aerobic method
content: Organic material is decomposed in the presence of air.
Turning is used to facilitate decomposition.
The source states decomposition ordinarily completes in about 4–5 months.
In heavy rainfall or high-water-table areas, heaps may be prepared above ground.

sections.heading: Anaerobic method
content: Uses a pit with compacted layers of farm residues.
Fresh cow dung, ash and water are added.
The pit is filled and decomposition proceeds without regular aeration.

topics.title: Vermicompost
topics.definition: Compost produced through the feeding and activity of earthworms on organic waste.

sections.heading: Process
content: Earthworms feed on waste organic material.
Organic matter is converted into vermicompost.
The source describes a harvesting and separation process after about four months.
The compost is dried in shade and sieved.
Earthworms are collected for the next preparation cycle.

sections.heading: Handling
content: Water is supplied as required during preparation.
Finished compost is packed in suitable polythene or laminated bags.

topics.title: Green Manuring
topics.definition: Ploughing or incorporating green plant material into soil to add organic matter and nutrients.

sections.heading: Benefits
content: Recycles nutrients.
Adds organic matter.
Reduces nutrient leaching.
Can improve crop yield.
Improves soil fertility.
Improves soil structure.
Helps prevent soil erosion.
Can aid weed control.

sections.heading: Green-leaf manuring
content: Uses green leaves and tender twigs from shrubs and trees.
Material may be collected from bunds, wastelands and nearby areas.
Examples include Glyricidia, Sesbania speciosa and Karanj.

sections.heading: In situ practice
content: Green-manure crops are incorporated into the soil at a suitable stage.
Legumes and nitrogen-fixing plants are especially useful.

topics.title: Farming System
topics.definition: A holistic farm-management approach integrating crops and allied enterprises so that outputs or wastes of one enterprise become inputs for another.

sections.heading: Examples
content: Crops.
Dairy.
Poultry.
Fishery.
Sericulture.
Piggery.
Apiary.
Tree crops.

sections.heading: Integration examples
content: Dairy dung and urine can produce FYM or compost.
Crop straw can feed dairy cattle.
Mulberry leaves feed silkworms.
Maize grain can be used as poultry feed.

sections.heading: Objective
content: Optimize production through efficient input use.
Maintain environmental quality.
Support national goals and farm-household needs.

topics.title: Principles and Scope of Farming System
topics.definition: Farming-system planning integrates resource, enterprise, economic and environmental considerations.

sections.heading: Overall objectives
content: Identify existing farming systems.
Develop models combining main and allied enterprises.
Optimize utilization and conservation of resources.
Maintain sustainable production without resource damage.
Increase farm-household profitability through complementary enterprises.

sections.heading: Scope factors
content: Soil and climate.
Land, labour and capital availability.
Current resource utilization.
Economics of the proposed system.
Farmer's managerial skill.

sections.heading: Enterprise-selection factors
content: Local soil and climate.
Farmer resources.
Existing resource use.
System economics.
Managerial skill.
Local social customs.

topics.title: Farming System Research (FSR)
topics.definition: A participatory research approach based on interdependence among farming-system components and the natural environment.

sections.heading: Core idea
content: Farmers participate in identifying research problems.
Farmers participate in testing possible solutions.
Technology should be evaluated beyond technical performance.
Research should be grounded in small-farmer conditions.

topics.title: Characteristics of Farming System
topics.definition: Features that make farming-system research and development farmer-oriented, location-specific and sustainability-focused.

sections.heading: Characteristics
content: Farmer-oriented and holistic.
Effective farmer participation.
Problem-solving approach.
Dynamic system.
Gender sensitive.
Responsible to society.
Environmental sustainability.
Location-specific technology.
Diversified enterprises to reduce environmental risk.

sections.heading: Additional characteristics
content: Bottom-up approach.
Focus on small and marginal farmers.
Extensive on-farm activities.
Collaboration between farmers and scientists.
Focus on actual adoption.
Recognizes interdependence among multiple clients.

topics.title: Objectives of Farming System
topics.definition: Production, income, employment, resource-use and environmental objectives achieved through integrated enterprises.

sections.heading: Objectives
content: Increase productivity per unit area and time.
Improve profitability through complementary enterprises.
Promote balanced food production.
Improve environmental safety.
Provide income or cash flow throughout the year.
Help meet fodder requirements.
Help meet timber and fuel requirements.
Generate employment.
Create scope for agro-industries.
Improve input-use efficiency.
Reduce production risk through enterprise diversification.

topics.title: Determinants of Farming System
topics.definition: Physical, biological, resource and human factors that determine the type of farming system.

sections.heading: Factors
content: Physical and biological conditions set limits on suitable enterprises.
Quantity and quality of land, water and other resources influence choices.
Farmer goals and attitudes affect the system.
Resource availability and resource-use level shape enterprise combinations.

topics.title: Cropping System
topics.definition: Principles and practices of cropping and their interaction with farm resources, technology and environmental conditions.

sections.heading: Multiple cropping
content: Sequential cropping: two or more crops grown in sequence on the same field in a year.
Intercropping: two or more dissimilar crops grown simultaneously.

sections.heading: Types of intercropping
content: Mixed intercropping: simultaneous crops without distinct rows.
Row intercropping: crops arranged in different rows.
Strip intercropping: crops grown in strips wide enough for independent management.
Relay intercropping: crops introduced in sequence so growth cycles overlap.

sections.heading: Other terms
content: Monoculture: repetitive growing of a sole crop.
Diversification and multiple cropping can help distribute production risk.

topics.title: Dairy Integration in Farming System
topics.definition: Integration of dairy livestock with cropping to diversify income, recycle nutrients and reduce production risk.

sections.heading: Benefits
content: Livestock diversification helps reduce risk.
Forage crops transfer nutrients within the farm.
Dung can be used as crop manure.
Crop residues provide livestock feed.

sections.heading: Cattle groups
content: Draft breeds.
Dairy breeds.
Dual-purpose breeds.
Exotic breeds.
Buffaloes.

sections.heading: Feed groups
content: Roughages: legumes, non-legume hays, straw and silage.
Concentrates: grains and grain/oilseed by-products.
Vitamin and mineral mixtures may supplement rations.

topics.title: Biogas / Gobar Gas Plant
topics.definition: A farm enterprise that converts animal dung and organic material into biogas and nutrient-rich slurry.

sections.heading: Types
content: Float-dome type, including KVIC models.
Fixed-dome type.

sections.heading: Technical points from source
content: Dry residual sludge contains approximately N 1.4–1.8%, P2O5 1.1–2.0% and K2O 0.8–1.2%.
Fresh dung gas yield is stated as about 0.04–0.1 m³ per kg per day, depending on temperature.
Gas production is highest around 30–35°C.
Production decreases sharply below 10°C.
One m³ of biogas is stated as equivalent to about 0.62 litres of kerosene.

topics.title: Sheep and Goat Rearing
topics.definition: A livestock enterprise suitable for diverse agro-climatic conditions and small-farm resource bases.

sections.heading: Advantages
content: High adaptability to different agro-climatic conditions.
Disease tolerance is noted in the source.
Multiple kids and relatively fast growth support production.
Provides employment through the year.
Small and marginal farmers can maintain animals with available fodder.

sections.heading: Feed
content: Green fodder includes legumes and cereals.
Crop residues can be used with suitable treatment or supplementation.
Concentrates include grains, bran, oilseed products and other feed materials.

topics.title: Poultry Farming
topics.definition: A livestock enterprise integrated into farming systems for eggs, meat, income and nutrient recycling.

sections.heading: Management
content: Day-old chicks are commonly used to start a unit.
Poultry houses need ventilation, water and power.
The site should be well drained and protected from floodwater.
Shed width is stated as not exceeding about 25–33 feet.

sections.heading: Feed and cost
content: The source states feed may account for 70–75% of poultry-farming expenditure.
Maize, rice bran and groundnut cake are examples of feed ingredients in an IFS model.

topics.title: Fisheries in Farming System
topics.definition: Fish culture integrated with crops and livestock to use farm water resources and recycle nutrients.

sections.heading: Fish species and feeding niches
content: Catla is described as a fast-growing Indian major carp and a surface/vegetation feeder.
Rohu is a column feeder.
Calbasu is a bottom feeder on detritus.
Mrigal is also associated with bottom feeding.
Silver carp mainly feeds on phytoplankton near the surface.
Grass carp feeds on aquatic plants and cut grass.

sections.heading: Integration
content: Fish ponds can receive nutrient-rich wastes from poultry or livestock.
Water availability and pond location are important for IFS planning.

topics.title: Bee Keeping / Apiculture
topics.definition: Management of honey bees for honey and other products while supporting crop pollination.

sections.heading: Bee species
content: Apis cerana is better acclimatized to higher Himalayan areas.
Apis mellifera and Apis dorsata are described as more profitable in plains.

sections.heading: Management
content: Beekeepers should know local nectar and pollen sources.
Nectar sources include tamarind, mango, guava and many fruit crops.
Pollen sources include maize, sorghum, millets, sunflower and palm.

sections.heading: Timing
content: The source identifies arrival of suitable nectar/pollen sources as important for starting beekeeping.

topics.title: Sericulture
topics.definition: Integrated production involving mulberry cultivation, silkworm rearing and silk reeling.

sections.heading: Core terms
content: Moriculture = cultivation of mulberry.
Mulberry is the chief food plant for the mulberry silkworm, Bombyx mori.
Sericulture includes mulberry cultivation, silkworm rearing and silk reeling.

sections.heading: Source details
content: The source states about 240 thousand ha under mulberry in India.
Silk production contributes to rural socio-economic development in some areas.
Silk goods are exported to multiple international markets.

topics.title: Agroforestry in Farming System
topics.definition: Integrated land management combining trees with crops, animals or other agricultural enterprises.

sections.heading: Purpose
content: Supports integrated and self-sustained land management.
Can supply fuel, fodder, fruit and timber.
Can support soil conservation and nutrient cycling.

sections.heading: Agri-horticultural system
content: Fruit trees are combined with short-duration arable crops.
Also called food-cum-fruit system.
Fruit-tree examples: guava, pomegranate, custard apple, sapota and mango.
Pulses are important arable crops for this system.

sections.heading: Alley cropping
content: Food crops are grown in alleys formed by tree or shrub hedgerows.

sections.heading: Tree farming
content: Useful where arable crops are less profitable.
Dryland farmers may prefer trees because of labour scarcity and drought-related crop failure.

topics.title: Other Integrated Farm Enterprises
topics.definition: Additional enterprises that can diversify farming systems.

sections.heading: Enterprises listed
content: Rabbit rearing.
Duck rearing.
Turkey rearing.
Piggery.
Mushroom cultivation.

sections.heading: Mushroom cultivation
content: Mushroom is an edible fungus.
It can use agricultural residues and fit into integrated systems.

topics.title: IFS Model for Wetland Situation
topics.definition: An integrated rice-based system combining crop, fish, poultry and mushroom enterprises.

sections.heading: Model components
content: Rice-based cropping.
Fish culture.
Poultry.
Mushroom production.

sections.heading: Example model
content: Cropping area: 0.36 ha.
Fish pond: 0.04 ha.
Fish pond depth: 1.5 m.
Fish stocking: about 7,500 fingerlings/ha.
Poultry shed placed near the fish pond.
Poultry droppings fall into the fish pond.
Oyster mushroom is produced using rice straw.

sections.heading: Economic result in source
content: Net profit reported: Rs. 11,755.
Conventional cropping comparison: Rs. 6,335.
Additional employment: 174 man-days.

topics.title: IFS Model: Tamil Nadu Cauvery Delta Zone
topics.definition: A rice–poultry–fish integrated system designed for a canal-irrigated rice-growing zone.

sections.heading: System
content: One-hectare model.
Fish pond: 0.04 ha.
Cropping: rice–rice–cotton on 0.76 ha.
Cropping: rice–rice–maize on 0.20 ha.
Maize supplies a major poultry-feed component.

sections.heading: Poultry and fish
content: Poultry unit uses Babcock and hybrid layer birds in the source model.
Feed includes maize, rice bran and groundnut cake.
Fish pond is located near the poultry shed.
Fish stocking density: about 10,000 fingerlings/ha.
Fish harvesting begins after about six and a half months.

sections.heading: Economic result
content: Net return reported: Rs. 17,200.
Employment generated: 385 man-days.

topics.title: IFS Model for Irrigated Situation
topics.definition: A one-hectare integrated model combining crops, fodder, dairy, biogas and mushroom production.

sections.heading: Cropping components
content: Cotton–green gram–maize + fodder cowpea–Bellary onion: 0.56 ha.
Wheat–sunflower–maize + fodder cowpea–summer cotton + green gram: 0.11 ha.
Grass Bajra Napier: 0.15 ha.
Lucerne: 0.05 ha.
Leucaena on bunds: 0.05 ha.
Total: 1.00 ha.

sections.heading: Farmstead
content: Dairy: 3 Jersey cows + 2 calves.
Biogas: 2 m³ capacity.
Mushroom production: 1.5–2.0 kg/ha as stated in the source.

sections.heading: Results
content: Mean revenue: Rs. 34,600/ha under IFS.
Conventional comparison: Rs. 13,950.
Employment: about 770 man-days/year.
Crop by-products are recycled into dairy feed.
Dung is recycled through the biogas unit.

topics.title: Paddy-Cum-Fish Culture
topics.definition: Rice production integrated with fish culture in water-retaining paddy fields.

sections.heading: Suitable conditions
content: Paddy fields remain flooded for about 3–8 months.
Low-lying fields with good water availability are preferred.
Soil should retain water and be fertile.

sections.heading: Fish species
content: Cyprinus carpio var. communis: scale carp.
Cyprinus carpio var. specularis: mirror carp.
Cyprinus carpio var. nudus: leather carp.

sections.heading: Field preparation
content: Construct strong bunds to retain water and prevent fish escape.
Level the field.
Provide irrigation and drainage channels.
Use inlets and outlets for water management.
Stock fish about 10–15 days after rice transplantation.

topics.title: Management and Production of Paddy-Cum-Fish Culture
topics.definition: Water, nutrient, stocking, harvesting and marketing practices for integrated rice-fish production.

sections.heading: Water and inputs
content: Water can be diverted from streams through wooden or bamboo barriers.
Organic fertilizers include poultry droppings, pig excreta, cow dung and plant wastes.
The source specifies no chemical insecticide, pesticide or fertilizer during the described integrated system.

sections.heading: Stocking
content: Fish seed rate: about 2,500 fish/ha.
Fish rearing period: 3–6 months.
Paddy rearing period: 5–7 months.

sections.heading: Harvest
content: 3–4 months fish culture: about 200–300 kg/ha reported.
5–6 months fish culture: about 400–500 kg/ha reported.
Water is drained through outlets before fish harvesting.
Paddy is harvested after fish harvesting.

sections.heading: Production and marketing
content: Paddy production is reported as about 3,500–4,500 kg/ha.
Fish may be sold live or fresh in local markets.
Source reports live fish at Rs.120/kg and fresh fish at Rs.100/kg during the cited period.
Prices fluctuate with season.

topics.title: Groundwater Management
topics.definition: Management of groundwater extraction and recharge to avoid depletion and support sustainable irrigation.

sections.heading: Problems
content: Increasing wells can increase extraction from limited aquifers.
Excess extraction lowers the groundwater table.
Over-irrigation can accumulate harmful salts.

sections.heading: Sustainable approach
content: Maximize groundwater recharge.
Minimize surface runoff.
Use conjunctive surface- and groundwater management.
Use recharge wells, check dams and percolation ponds where suitable.
